prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I have moved from B022 to B008. The lattice clock is a single, sharply defined invention: a magic-wavelength optical lattice cancels Doppler, recoil and lattice-induced shifts while many neutral atoms are interrogated in parallel, which took optical clocks from the 1e-16 regime to about 1e-18. It has been reproduced independently in Sr, Yb and Hg and is used in routine international comparisons, so maturity is not in question. It also opens relativistic geodesy, tests of varying constants and many-body clock physics, which answers the charge that it is only a precision gain. The credit maps onto proposal and first realisation (Katori) and record accuracy and many-body operation (Ye), and the citation can be kept on the lattice concept itself.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems, which includes ion clocks. Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work sits close to the 2005 recognition, and the citation must be drafted on the lattice concept and not on optical timekeeping in general. The credit also leaves out PTB, SYRTE, NIST and ytterbium and mercury groups, so the two names are a judgment about decisive contribution, not the whole field. The pending redefinition of the second is a timing question that I do not think should carry weight in either direction.

responses.point: Argues that the lattice concept is a different idea from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and that the citation should stay on the lattice clock itself.
responses.response: In round 1 I said the overlap argument cuts against B008 as much as against B022, and I still think it applies. But your and Lindroth's formulation answers it better than I had allowed: the comb is a counting ruler, Wineland's work is control of single quantum systems, and neither covers many neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice with shifts cancelled. That is a distinct invention. I also now accept your point that the overlap is more serious for B022 than I argued, because the 2012 prize already covered the experimental foundation I was relying on. I agree the citation must not widen to comb or ultrastable-laser contributors.

responses.point: Says Blatt's share is contestable given Wineland's 2012 prize and the NIST and Innsbruck first-gate claims, so a trio with one disputed slot is weaker than a pair with a clear split.
responses.response: This is the point that moved me. I had treated the Blatt allocation as a qualification that the 30-year Cirac-Zoller line could absorb, but a prize that credits the proposal cleanly and the experimental half only by a judgment call is weaker than one where inventors are identifiable from the papers. A theory-only Cirac-Zoller prize would leave the realisation unrecognised, which I cannot support. I agree B022 is not far behind and should stay as my first alternative.

responses.point: Holds that the Wineland prize already covered the experimental control of trapped ions, that the first entangling gates came substantially from NIST and Innsbruck, and that B008 has a cleaner invention-to-demonstration chain.
responses.response: I accept the substance of your argument. Where I still differ slightly is on weight of the 2012 overlap: Wineland and Haroche were recognised for controlling individual quantum systems, whereas Cirac and Zoller concern the logic of computation, so the overlap does not make B022 improper. It does, however, make the experimental credit harder to fix, and on that criterion B008 is clearly the safer prize. On timing I agree with you that the pending SI redefinition should not make us wait; the achievement is mature as it stands.

responses.point: Notes that Hall and Hansch recognised the comb as a ruler and Wineland single-ion control, neither a neutral-atom lattice at a magic wavelength, and that the credit should say the prize is for the invention and its realisation, not the whole field of optical clocks.
responses.response: Your assessment from the atomic-structure side, that the magic-wavelength condition and systematic shifts are well understood and independently reproduced, is what lets me trust the 1e-18 claim, and it lowers my main worry about the clock. I agree with your wording point: the citation should name the invention and development of the lattice clock and not imply that the allocation covers all of optical-clock metrology. I would also join you in not adding names to settle the credit question.

responses.point: Maintains that B035 is a rare prediction-plus-discovery pairing with exceptional breadth, that a prize can precede mechanism, and that B008 is mainly a large precision gain.
responses.response: I agree the discovery of the magic-angle platform is not in dispute and that we have honoured effects before the mechanism was understood. My position is not that mechanism must be settled, but that the credited names do not cover the decisive 2018 experimental work (Cao and collaborators, and parallel groups), so the attribution is not yet fixed. On weight, I do not think the clock is only precision: relativistic geodesy, tests of varying constants and many-body clock physics are physics, but I accept your view that B035 would be the more novel result in a later year.

responses.point: Takes the novelty objection seriously and wants the committee to say explicitly why the lattice architecture is a distinct invention, while holding B056 as the larger scientific event.
responses.response: I agree that the distinctness must be stated and not assumed, and I think it is answerable: neutral-atom, Doppler-free, many-atom interrogation is neither the comb nor single-ion control. On B056 I do not dispute that the Higgs observation is the larger event, but the three-from-four allocation among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee is the same kind of contestable credit that moved me away from B022, so I would not add it as a second part this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which I judge it is but which remains the most contestable point.
Whether Katori and Ye adequately cover the decisive credit given PTB, SYRTE, NIST and the early lattice-clock proposals, a judgment I cannot verify from the supplied files.
Whether Blatt, Monroe or another experimentalist would be the right third name if the committee returned to B022 later.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of Katori, Ye, Cirac, Zoller, Blatt or the other credited names for B008, B022 and B012 appears among my documented co-authors, supervisors or institutions. My 2024 comments on machine learning were made as a university expert and are not relevant to these candidates.
